title: Free-volume origin of diverging direct correlations in hard crystals: insights from an exact one-dimensional model
abstract: Second order direct correlation functions in three-dimensional hard-sphere crystals have much larger amplitudes (of the order of $1/n_{\mathrm{vac}}$ where $n_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacancy concentration) and a more strongly structured spatial form of apparent shorter range than their liquid-state counterparts. We separate the two underlying questions---why the correlations are large and why they have the form they do---using the exact one-dimensional Percus functional for hard rods. A periodic crystal-like density is represented by Gaussian peaks with occupation probability $q=1-n_{\mathrm{vac}}$. The relevant thermodynamic quantity is the local insertion free volume $A(x)$. Its minimum can be written as $A_{\mathrm{min}} =Δ_{αa}+(1-Δ_{αa})n_{\mathrm{vac}}$, where $Δ_{αa}$ is the residual free volume at full occupation caused by finite localization (characterized by a width parameter $α$) and lattice spacing $a$. The first and second direct correlations therefore contain the singular dependences $c^{(1)}\sim\ln A_{\mathrm{min}} $ and $c^{(2)} \sim-1/A_{\mathrm{min}} $. The observed $1/n_{\mathrm{vac}}$ dependence is the vacancy-dominated limit $n_{\mathrm{vac}}\ggΔ_{αa}$, rather than the most general result. The spatial form of $c^{(2)}$ has a separate geometrical origin: the hard-rod weight functions select configurations in which exclusion intervals and their boundaries intersect regions of small free volume. This produces plateaus, edges, and localized ridges tied to the underlying periodic density. A numerical solution of the inhomogeneous Ornstein--Zernike equation shows how these singular direct correlations are redistributed in the total and pair correlations. The model provides a minimal free-volume explanation for both the magnitude and the lattice-specific form of crystalline direct correlation functions.
summary: This work uses an exact 1D hard-rod model within statistical mechanics to explain the anomalous behavior of direct correlation functions in crystalline solids. It shows that these divergences are not arbitrary but arise directly from the geometry and scarcity of local free volume within the crystal lattice. The findings provide a minimal, physically grounded explanation for both the magnitude and structure of these key thermodynamic quantities.
main_problem: The study aims to explain the unusually large amplitudes and specific spatial structure of second-order direct correlation functions in hard-sphere crystals compared to their liquid counterparts.
main_result: The paper establishes that both the magnitude (scaling as $1/n_{vac}$) and the lattice-specific form of these correlations are fundamentally controlled by the minimum local insertion free volume, $A_{\min}$.
method: The authors employ an exact one-dimensional model for hard rods within a classical Density Functional Theory framework to derive theoretical scaling laws.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a crystal of hard spheres (approximated by hard rods in 1D) characterized by a periodic, crystal-like density profile. The analysis focuses on the local insertion free volume $A(x)$ as the key thermodynamic quantity.
key_observables: Second direct correlation function ($c^{(2)}$), first direct correlation function ($c^{(1)}$), and the local insertion free volume ($A(x)$).
important_parameters: Vacancy concentration ($n_{vac}$), residual free volume ($\Delta\alpha_a$), and the minimum local free volume ($A_{\min}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on using an exactly solvable 1D model and imposing a periodic density profile, rather than modeling the full crystallization transition.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate density profiles showing how $A$ changes between broad and sharply localized peaks. Other figures compare $c^{(2)}$ for sharp versus broad peaks, demonstrating geometric selectivity related to free volume.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the relationship between direct correlations and local free volume in 1D (using the Ornstein-Zernike equation). It then analyzes how this mechanism dictates both the magnitude ($c^{(2)} \sim -1/A_{\min}$) and the spatial structure of the correlation functions.
why_interesting: While focused on classical hard-body systems, the rigorous connection drawn between singular thermodynamic quantities (like $c^{(2)}$) and geometric constraints (like minimal free volume) provides a powerful theoretical template applicable to understanding correlations in quantum many-body systems near phase boundaries or confinement.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Density profiles and corresponding weighted densities for a broad peak (a) and a sharply localized peak (b) for nvac = 1 × 10−2. The weighted packing fraction n1 determines the local insertion free volume A = 1 −n1.

FIG. 2. Crossover for the inverse minimal free volume implied by Equation (20). The minimum insertion free volume follows Amin ≃nvac only while the vacancy contribution exceeds the residual free volume ∆αa. The corresponding inverse-free- volume amplification saturates at 1/∆αa when nvac ≪∆αa.

FIG. 3. First direct correlation function for a single broad density peak (a) and a sharply localized peak (b). The strong vacancy dependence in panel (b) reflects the regime Amin ≃ nvac; the weak dependence in panel (a) reflects saturation at a finite residual free volume.

FIG. 4. Full second direct correlation function for sharply localized peaks (a, b), and broad density peaks (c, d) at nvac = 1×10−2. The lattice spacing was either a/σ = 1.03 for (a, c) and a/σ = 1.1 for (b, d). The strict support (marked by the dashed region) remains fixed by the rod length, but the dominant large-amplitude contribution becomes concentrated along geometrically selected regions in the sharp case. For the numerics, a lattice with five density peaks has been used, shown is only the region around the middle peak.

FIG. 5. Numerical solution of the inhomogeneous Ornstein– Zernike equation for a sharply localized profile at nvac = 1 × 10−2 and a = 1.03. The dashed and full lines show the different support in the unit cell, cf. Figure 6.
